title: Typing NestJS patterns
subtitle: DTO classes, pipes, guards, decorators, config

cards.front: What Nest + TypeScript patterns do interviews probe?
cards.meaning: Nest sits on TypeScript plus Express (or Fastify) plus decorators. The patterns that matter: DTO classes as the joint compile-time type and runtime validation source of truth; why class not interface/type; generic services/repositories; custom param decorators; typed guards/interceptors; and ConfigService.get<T>() so config is not secretly any.

cards.front: What TypeScript topics does Nest DTO typing assume?
cards.meaning: Type erasure / structural typing, declaration merging (Request.user), and generics.

cards.front: What dual role do Nest DTO classes play?
cards.meaning: They are the joint compile-time type and runtime validation source of truth, via class-validator and class-transformer.

cards.front: Why Nest DTOs are classes, not interfaces?
cards.meaning: Interfaces and types erase. Decorators like @IsEmail() need a real runtime target so metadata can attach via reflect-metadata. A class compiles to a constructor function, so it carries both compile-time checking and runtime validation metadata. ValidationPipe reads that metadata; an interface leaves nothing to decorate.

cards.front: What does ValidationPipe reflect on a DTO class?
cards.meaning: Decorator metadata on the prototype/constructor — rules like “this property should be an email / min length 8.” The pipe reflects that and runs checks. No class means no place to hang those rules, so no automatic validation from decorators.

cards.front: What shape is an HTTP body before ValidationPipe?
cards.meaning: A plain object, untrusted. Types on @Body() do not make it a validated instance by themselves.

cards.front: What is the ValidationPipe DTO pipeline?
cards.meaning: HTTP body arrives as a plain object. With transform: true, class-transformer instantiates the DTO class. class-validator reads decorator metadata and validates. The controller method then receives a typed DTO instance, or Nest throws 400.
cards.example: app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true }));

cards.front: What does ValidationPipe transform: true do?
cards.meaning: It turns the plain JSON object into a real class instance via class-transformer, so decorator metadata and validation run on a CreateUserDto (not a leftover POJO).

cards.front: What does ValidationPipe whitelist: true do?
cards.meaning: It strips properties without decorator metadata, which helps block unexpected fields from reaching persistence.
cards.notes: Skipping whitelist is a common mistake — extra body keys can be accepted.

cards.front: Does @Body() dto: CreateUserDto validate without a pipe?
cards.meaning: No. Without the pipe plus a class DTO, dto: CreateUserDto is only a TypeScript annotation — erasure means nothing validates at runtime. You need ValidationPipe (or manual parse) for enforcement.

cards.front: Is Omit<User,'passwordHash'> enough to hide a hash in JSON?
cards.meaning: No. Compile-time Omit only constrains what you write in TS. If you return userEntity and Nest JSON-serializes the real object, passwordHash can still leak. Safer: a response DTO class plus ClassSerializerInterceptor with @Exclude() / @Expose() from class-transformer.

cards.front: Interview line: is type safety an output filter?
cards.meaning: Type safety alone is not an output filter. TypeScript DTO / Omit types catch mistakes in your code; serializer plus @Exclude strips sensitive fields at runtime before JSON.

cards.front: What runtime tools strip sensitive response fields in Nest?
cards.meaning: ClassSerializerInterceptor plus @Exclude() / @Expose() from class-transformer on entity/DTO fields, usually together with a response DTO class — not Omit alone.

cards.front: Why CrudService<TEntity, TCreate, TUpdate>?
cards.meaning: Generics keep entity, create DTO, and update DTO roles distinct: CreateUserDto is inbound and validated, User/entity is the persistence shape, UserResponseDto is outbound safe fields. Avoid one any-ish “user” object for the whole stack.

cards.front: Repository<User> — what is User at runtime?
cards.meaning: The generic parameter is the entity class — a runtime construct for the ORM — separate from HTTP DTO classes used at the boundary.

cards.front: How should createParamDecorator be typed for CurrentUser?
cards.meaning: Give the factory a return type of User so controllers receive a documented type, not any. The decorator only reads request.user — a guard or middleware must set it, and Express declaration merging makes Request.user known to TS.
cards.example: export const CurrentUser = createParamDecorator((data: unknown, ctx: ExecutionContext): User => { ... return request.user as User; });

cards.front: What is the data argument to createParamDecorator?
cards.meaning: It is the optional argument to @CurrentUser('email')-style usage. Type it if you use it, e.g. data: keyof User | undefined.

cards.front: What goes wrong if @CurrentUser() is typed User but no guard sets req.user?
cards.meaning: The type lies. The decorator only reads request.user; without a guard or middleware assigning it, you get a typed hole at runtime. Pair the decorator with a guard that sets user and with Request.user augmentation.

cards.front: What does a Nest guard implement?
cards.meaning: CanActivate — implement canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean | Promise<boolean>. Return true to allow, false or throw to block.

cards.front: What is ExecutionContext for?
cards.meaning: An abstract wrapper around the current request. Use switchToHttp(), switchToRpc(), or switchToWs() to get the right request. Typing getRequest<Request>() (or a custom request type) avoids any on req.

cards.front: Are Nest guards just untyped Express middleware?
cards.meaning: No. Nest gives ExecutionContext so you can switch transport and type the request instead of treating guards and interceptors as untyped Express middleware.

cards.front: What is the NestInterceptor signature?
cards.meaning: intercept(context: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler) returns Observable. next.handle() is an Observable (RxJS) of the handler result. Map or transform responses here, or use ClassSerializerInterceptor for DTO serialization.

cards.front: How much RxJS do you need for interceptor interviews?
cards.meaning: You do not need deep RxJS. Know the signatures and that interceptors wrap the stream before and after the handler.

cards.front: Does config.get<number>('PORT') parse the env value?
cards.meaning: No. get<T> is a type assertion-shaped generic — it does not coerce strings from env. Use transform in config validation (Joi/Zod/class-validator on a config class) for real parsing. The generic documents intent and improves call-site checking; validation still belongs at config load.

cards.front: get vs getOrThrow on ConfigService?
cards.meaning: get<T>(key) is typically T | undefined. getOrThrow<T>(key) is for keys that must exist, e.g. getOrThrow<string>('DATABASE_URL').

cards.front: What happens if you omit <T> on config.get?
cards.meaning: Values are often loosely typed. Prefer get<T> / getOrThrow<T> with an explicit T, or a typed config object so keys are not free-form strings everywhere.

cards.front: How else can you type Nest config besides get<T>?
cards.meaning: A typed config object via a custom config factory / ConfigType<typeof appConfig> so keys are not free-form strings at every call site.

cards.front: What is the Nest request/response typing picture end to end?
cards.meaning: HTTP JSON → ValidationPipe plus CreateUserDto (class + decorators) → controller (@Body dto: CreateUserDto) → service generics / business logic → entity / DB → response DTO plus serializer (strip secrets) → JSON out.

cards.front: How does typed CurrentUser fit the auth path?
cards.meaning: A guard sets req.user, you declare global Express.Request.user via declaration merging, then @CurrentUser() user: User in the controller.

cards.front: How does type erasure force DTO classes?
cards.meaning: Interfaces cannot hold decorator metadata because they vanish at compile time. reflect-metadata plus decorators on a class constructor are what ValidationPipe and the serializer can actually read.

cards.front: How does declaration merging connect to CurrentUser?
cards.meaning: Merging Express.Request with a user field is what makes request.user known to TypeScript when the decorator and controllers read it.

cards.front: Where do generics show up in Nest typing?
cards.meaning: CrudService-style entity/DTO parameters, Repository<Entity>, and ConfigService get<T> / getOrThrow<T>.

cards.front: Does Omit or Pick strip passwordHash at runtime?
cards.meaning: No. Omit / Pick are compile-time only. They are not a runtime exclude of passwordHash from JSON.
